entries.name: Rama’s Journey
entries.summary: Tradition tells how Prince Rama of Ayodhya, exiled for fourteen years, crossed India with Sita and his brother Lakshmana. When Ravana, king of Lanka, carried Sita away, Rama allied with Hanuman and the monkey army (vanara sena), bridged the sea and won her back. Valmiki’s Sanskrit epic is the oldest telling; many regional versions followed.

entries.name: The Mahabharata
entries.summary: Tradition’s great war epic, attributed to the sage Vyasa. The five Pandava brothers and their cousins the Kauravas fight for the throne of Hastinapura, ending in eighteen days of battle at Kurukshetra. Within it sits the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna’s counsel to Arjuna on duty. At about 100,000 verses, it is among the longest poems ever composed.

entries.name: The Bhagavad Gita
entries.summary: Tradition’s Song of the Lord, 700 verses in the Mahabharata’s sixth book. On the battlefield of Kurukshetra, Arjuna refuses to fight his kin, and his charioteer Krishna teaches him to act from duty without attachment to results, through knowledge, action and devotion (bhakti). It became one of Hinduism’s most read and most commented-on texts.

entries.name: The Life of Krishna
entries.summary: In tradition, Krishna is born in a prison in Mathura, raised among cowherds in Vrindavan and later rules from Dwarka on the western coast. Worshipped as an avatar of Vishnu, he is the playful child and flute-playing cowherd of devotional poetry, and Arjuna’s charioteer and teacher in the Bhagavad Gita. The Bhagavata Purana tells his life most fully.

entries.name: The Bhagavata Purana
entries.summary: One of the eighteen great Puranas, in twelve books and about 18,000 verses, usually dated to about the 9th or 10th century, though the date is debated. Its tenth book, Krishna’s life, is the fullest telling of his childhood in Vraja, and it became the central scripture of devotion (bhakti) to Krishna.

entries.name: The Battle of the Ten Kings
entries.summary: Hymns in the Rigveda’s seventh book tell how Sudas, king of the Bharatas, guided by his priest Vasishtha, defeats an alliance of ten kings on the Parushni (Ravi), where many of his enemies drown. Whether it records a real battle is debated, but it is often read as the rise of the Bharatas over the other clans.

entries.name: The Churning of the Ocean
entries.summary: In Puranic tradition, the gods (devas) and demons (asuras) churn the ocean of milk for the nectar of immortality (amrita), with Mount Mandara as the churning rod and the serpent Vasuki as the rope. Vishnu, as a tortoise, holds the mountain up. Poison, treasures and the goddess Lakshmi rise from the sea before the nectar.

entries.name: Indus Valley civilisation
entries.note: The cities flourished from about 2600 to 1900 BCE.
entries.summary: One of the world’s first urban civilisations, alongside Egypt and Mesopotamia. Cities such as Harappa, Mohenjo-daro and Dholavira had planned streets, brick drains and standard weights, and traded as far as Mesopotamia. Its seals carry a script no one has deciphered, and no ruler’s name survives. The cities declined after about 1900 BCE, probably with shifting rivers and climate.

entries.name: Vedic period
entries.note: Dates come from the texts and are debated; the Rigveda is usually placed about 1500 to 1200 BCE.
entries.summary: The age of the Vedas, India’s oldest sacred texts, composed in Sanskrit and passed down by memory for centuries before they were written. Early Vedic people herded cattle in the Punjab; later they farmed the Ganga plain and formed kingdoms such as Kuru and Panchala. The fire ritual (yajna) and early forms of the caste order (varna) took shape.

entries.name: The great kingdoms (Mahajanapadas)
entries.summary: Buddhist and Jain texts list sixteen great kingdoms and republics (mahajanapadas) across northern India, among them Magadha, Kosala, Vatsa and the Vajji confederacy. Cities and the first coins appear on the Ganga plain. The Buddha and Mahavira taught in this age. Magadha, under kings such as Bimbisara and Ajatashatru, gradually swallowed its rivals.

entries.name: Nanda dynasty
entries.summary: The Nandas ruled Magadha from Pataliputra and built the largest kingdom in northern India of their time, famed in Greek and Indian sources for its huge army and wealth. Tradition names the founder Mahapadma Nanda and says he was of humble birth. The last Nanda king, Dhana Nanda in later tradition, was overthrown by Chandragupta Maurya.

entries.name: Maurya Empire
entries.summary: The first empire to rule most of the Indian subcontinent. Chandragupta, guided, tradition says, by Chanakya, overthrew the Nandas and won lands west of the Indus from Seleucus. His grandson Ashoka, shaken by the Kalinga war, preached a moral law (dhamma) in edicts carved on rocks and pillars from Afghanistan to Karnataka. His Sarnath lion capital is India’s national emblem.

entries.name: Kalinga War
entries.summary: Ashoka’s war against Kalinga, on India’s east coast in today’s Odisha. His own Thirteenth Rock Edict says 100,000 were killed and 150,000 carried away, numbers as the edict gives them, and records his remorse. It is the turning point of his reign: afterwards he turned from conquest to spreading a moral law (dhamma).

entries.name: Shunga dynasty
entries.summary: Founded by Pushyamitra Shunga, the Maurya commander who killed the last Maurya king, Brihadratha, about 185 BCE. The Shungas ruled a smaller kingdom across the Ganges valley and central India. Later Buddhist texts call Pushyamitra a persecutor of Buddhists, which historians debate. The carved stone railings of the stupa at Bharhut date from this period.

entries.name: Kushan Empire
entries.summary: Descended from the Yuezhi of Central Asia, the Kushans ruled from Bactria to the Ganges plain. Their greatest king, Kanishka, was a patron of Buddhism. Kushan lands sat across the Silk Road, linking India with China, Persia and Rome, and the Gandhara and Mathura schools of sculpture made some of the earliest images of the Buddha in human form.

entries.name: Gupta Empire
entries.summary: Often called India’s classical age. Chandragupta I founded the empire, Samudragupta expanded it across northern India, and Chandragupta II ruled at its height. Aryabhata wrote his astronomy and mathematics, the poet Kalidasa is usually placed in this age, and Sanskrit literature and temple building flourished. Hun invasions helped weaken the empire after about 500 CE.

entries.name: Harsha’s empire
entries.note: The reign of Harsha of the Pushyabhuti dynasty.
entries.summary: Harsha of the Pushyabhuti dynasty ruled much of northern India from Kannauj. He is known unusually well: his court poet Banabhatta wrote his life (the Harshacharita), and the Chinese pilgrim Xuanzang described his court and great Buddhist assemblies. Harsha wrote plays himself. His push south was stopped by the Chalukya king Pulakeshin II.

entries.name: Gurjara-Pratihara dynasty
entries.summary: The Gurjara-Pratiharas ruled much of northern India from Kannauj and held back Arab armies advancing from Sindh. For about two centuries they fought the Palas of Bengal and the Rashtrakutas of the Deccan for Kannauj and the Ganges plain, a contest historians call the tripartite struggle. Mihira Bhoja was their most powerful king.

entries.name: Pala Empire
entries.summary: The Palas ruled Bengal and Bihar for about four centuries. An inscription says the first king, Gopala, was chosen to end years of disorder; Dharmapala and Devapala made them a great power. Devout patrons of Buddhism, they supported the monastic universities of Nalanda and Vikramashila, whose teachers carried Buddhism to Tibet.

entries.name: Delhi Sultanate
entries.summary: Five dynasties ruled from Delhi in turn: the Mamluks, Khaljis, Tughlaqs, Sayyids and Lodis. They held off Mongol invasions, and under Alauddin Khalji and Muhammad bin Tughlaq reached deep into the south. The Qutb Minar, and the Persian and Indian culture that grew at their courts, including the poetry of Amir Khusrau, are among their legacies.

entries.name: First Battle of Panipat
entries.summary: Babur, a Timurid prince from Kabul, defeated Ibrahim Lodi, the last Delhi sultan, at Panipat, north of Delhi. Babur’s smaller army used field guns and matchlocks, among the first in India, with mounted archers on the flanks. Ibrahim Lodi died on the field. The victory ended the Delhi Sultanate and began the Mughal Empire.

entries.name: Mughal Empire
entries.summary: Founded by Babur, the Mughals ruled most of the subcontinent at their height. Akbar built an empire of alliances and religious tolerance, Shah Jahan built the Taj Mahal, and Aurangzeb pushed the empire to its widest. Their courts blended Persian and Indian art, music and language. After 1707 power passed to regional states; the British ended the dynasty in 1857.

entries.name: Company rule
entries.summary: The English East India Company, a trading company, became a ruling power after winning at Plassey in 1757 and gaining the right to collect Bengal’s revenue in 1765. With its own armies it conquered or made allies of most Indian states. The rebellion of 1857 ended Company rule, and the British Crown took over in 1858.

entries.name: British Raj
entries.summary: From 1858 the British Crown ruled India directly through a Viceroy, with hundreds of princely states under its authority. Railways, telegraphs and universities spread, alongside famines and heavy taxation. The Indian National Congress, founded in 1885, and leaders such as Gandhi, Nehru and Bose led the struggle for independence, won on 15 August 1947 with partition.

entries.name: Partition of India
entries.summary: In August 1947 British India was divided into India and Pakistan, with Punjab and Bengal split between them. An estimated 10 to 20 million people were displaced, one of the largest migrations in history. Estimates of the dead range from several hundred thousand to two million and are disputed. Its memory still shapes both countries.

entries.name: Satavahana dynasty
entries.note: When it began is disputed; some sources put it in the 3rd century BCE.
entries.summary: The Satavahanas ruled the Deccan from Pratishthana (Paithan) and grew rich on trade with Rome through western ports. Their most famous king, Gautamiputra Satakarni, defeated the Western Kshatrapas. They issued coins with portraits of their kings, and Buddhist monuments such as Amaravati and the cave monasteries at Karla and Nashik flourished in their time.

entries.name: Vakataka dynasty
entries.summary: The Vakatakas ruled the northern Deccan and were close allies of the Guptas: Prabhavatigupta, daughter of Chandragupta II, married into the dynasty and ruled as regent. Their lasting fame is Ajanta, where many of the finest Buddhist caves and wall paintings were made under King Harishena in the late 5th century.

entries.name: Chalukyas of Badami
entries.summary: The Chalukyas ruled the Deccan from Vatapi (Badami). Pulakeshin II, their greatest king, stopped Harsha’s advance south and fought the Pallavas, who later sacked Badami. They pioneered stone temple building in the Deccan: the rock-cut caves of Badami and the temples of Aihole and Pattadakal, which mix northern and southern styles.

entries.name: Rashtrakuta dynasty
entries.summary: The Rashtrakutas, ruling from Manyakheta, were for two centuries one of the strongest powers in India, fighting the Palas and Pratiharas for the Ganges plain. Krishna I had the Kailasa temple at Ellora carved from a single rock, top down. Amoghavarsha I was a patron of Kannada and Sanskrit literature. Arab travellers ranked their king among the world’s greatest.

entries.name: Western Chalukyas
entries.summary: Also called the Chalukyas of Kalyani. Tailapa II revived Chalukya rule after the Rashtrakutas fell, and the dynasty fought the Cholas for most of two centuries. Vikramaditya VI ruled for about fifty years and was celebrated by the poet Bilhana. Their ornate temples, such as those at Lakkundi and Itagi, led into the Hoysala style.

entries.name: Hoysala Empire
entries.summary: The Hoysalas rose in the hills of Karnataka and ruled from Dorasamudra (Halebidu). Vishnuvardhana made them a major power. They are remembered for their star-shaped temples, covered in fine soapstone carving, at Belur, Halebidu and Somanathapura. Raids by the Delhi Sultanate in the 14th century brought the kingdom to an end.

entries.name: Yadavas of Devagiri
entries.summary: The Yadavas, or Seunas, ruled the western Deccan from Devagiri, today’s Daulatabad. Their court encouraged Marathi, and the saint-poet Dnyaneshwar wrote his commentary on the Bhagavad Gita in their time. Alauddin Khalji’s raid on Devagiri in 1296 made them pay tribute to Delhi, and the kingdom was annexed in 1317.

entries.name: Bahmani Sultanate
entries.summary: Founded by Alauddin Hasan Bahman Shah, who rebelled against the Delhi Sultanate in 1347. The Bahmanis ruled the Deccan from Gulbarga and later Bidar, and fought Vijayanagara for the rich Raichur doab. Their minister Mahmud Gawan built a famous madrasa at Bidar. The kingdom broke up into five successor states, the Deccan Sultanates.

entries.name: Deccan Sultanates
entries.summary: Five kingdoms that grew out of the Bahmani Sultanate: Bijapur, Golconda, Ahmadnagar, Bidar and Berar. Together they defeated Vijayanagara at Talikota in 1565. Their courts blended Persian and Deccani culture and left the Gol Gumbaz at Bijapur and the Charminar at Hyderabad. The Mughal emperor Aurangzeb conquered the last of them, Golconda, in 1687.

entries.name: Battle of Talikota
entries.summary: Also called the Battle of Rakshasa-Tangadi. An alliance of the Deccan Sultanates defeated the army of Vijayanagara, led by its regent Aliya Rama Raya, who was captured and killed. The victors then sacked the capital, Vijayanagara (Hampi), which was never rebuilt. The empire survived, ruled from further south, but never recovered its strength.

entries.name: Maratha Empire
entries.summary: Shivaji, crowned in 1674, built a Maratha kingdom in the western Deccan, using hill forts and swift light cavalry against the Mughals and Bijapur. Under the Peshwas, chief ministers based at Pune, Maratha power spread across much of India in the 18th century. Defeat at Panipat in 1761 checked them, and the British defeated them in 1818.

entries.name: Third Battle of Panipat
entries.summary: Ahmad Shah Durrani’s Afghan army, with Indian allies including the Rohilla chief Najib ud-Daula and the nawab of Awadh, destroyed a Maratha army under Sadashivrao Bhau north of Delhi. Both the Bhau and the Peshwa’s heir were killed. Deaths are disputed estimates in the tens of thousands. The defeat checked Maratha expansion in the north for a decade.

entries.name: The Three Crowned Kings (early Tamil kingdoms)
entries.note: The Cheras, Cholas and Pandyas of the Sangam age.
entries.summary: The Cheras, Cholas and Pandyas ruled the far south in the Sangam age, named after the assemblies of poets that tradition places at Madurai. Sangam poetry in Tamil describes their kings, wars and ports. Through harbours such as Muziris and Arikamedu they traded pepper, pearls and cloth with Rome, which Roman coins and pottery found there confirm.

entries.name: Pallava dynasty
entries.summary: The Pallavas ruled from Kanchipuram and fought the Chalukyas of Badami for much of their history; Narasimhavarman I captured Badami in 642. They are remembered for their stone monuments: the rock-cut temples and Shore Temple at Mamallapuram (Mahabalipuram), and the Kailasanatha temple at Kanchipuram, early masterpieces of southern temple building.

entries.name: Chola Empire
entries.summary: The Cholas built one of the greatest powers in Indian history. Rajaraja I built the Brihadishvara temple at Thanjavur; his son Rajendra I sent an army to the Ganges and a navy against Srivijaya in Southeast Asia. Their bronze sculptures, such as Shiva as lord of the dance (Nataraja), and their village assemblies, recorded in inscriptions, are celebrated.

entries.name: Later Pandyas
entries.summary: The Pandyas of Madurai rose again as the Chola Empire weakened, and under Jatavarman Sundara Pandya became the leading power in the south. The Venetian traveller Marco Polo visited their coast and described its pearl fisheries. A war between brothers opened the way for a raid by the Delhi Sultanate, led by Malik Kafur in 1311, which broke their power.

entries.name: Vijayanagara Empire
entries.summary: Founded by the brothers Harihara and Bukka, the empire held southern India for about three centuries. Its capital, Vijayanagara (Hampi), amazed Persian and Portuguese visitors with its size and markets. Krishnadevaraya, its most celebrated king, was a poet and patron of Telugu and Kannada literature. Defeat at Talikota in 1565 led to the capital’s destruction.

entries.name: Nayakas of Madurai
entries.summary: The Nayakas began as Vijayanagara’s governors in Madurai and became independent as the empire weakened. Their greatest ruler, Tirumala Nayaka, built the palace that bears his name, and they enlarged the Meenakshi temple with its tall carved gateway towers (gopurams). Rani Mangammal ruled as regent. Chanda Sahib, for the Nawab of Arcot, ended their rule in 1736.

entries.name: Mysore under Hyder Ali and Tipu Sultan
entries.summary: Hyder Ali, a soldier who rose to command the Mysore army, took power from the Wodeyar kings in 1761. He and his son Tipu Sultan fought four wars against the East India Company, using iron-cased rockets that impressed the British. Tipu was killed defending Srirangapatna in 1799, and the Wodeyars were restored under British control.

entries.name: Sikh Empire
entries.summary: Ranjit Singh united the Sikh confederacies (misls), took Lahore in 1799 and built a kingdom across the Punjab, Kashmir and Peshawar. His army, trained partly by European officers, was among the strongest in Asia, and he covered the Harmandir Sahib at Amritsar in gold. After his death in 1839 the kingdom weakened, and Britain annexed it in 1849.

entries.name: Eastern Ganga dynasty
entries.note: An earlier Eastern Ganga line ruled from the 5th century; these dates are the later dynasty.
entries.summary: From Odisha the later Eastern Gangas ruled the old land of Kalinga. Anantavarman Chodaganga began the great Jagannath temple at Puri, and Narasimhadeva I built the Sun Temple at Konark, shaped as a giant stone chariot. They held off attacks from the sultans of Bengal until the Gajapati kings took over in 1434.

entries.name: Ahom kingdom
entries.summary: Founded by Sukaphaa, a Tai prince who crossed into the Brahmaputra valley in 1228, the Ahom kingdom ruled Assam for six centuries. Its court kept chronicles (buranjis). Its general Lachit Borphukan defeated a Mughal fleet at Saraighat in 1671. Weakened by civil war and Burmese invasions, it passed to the British in 1826.

entries.name: Minoan Crete
entries.summary: On Crete, a Bronze Age people built great palaces such as Knossos, with painted walls, light wells and huge storerooms, from about 2000 BCE. The archaeologist Arthur Evans named them Minoans after the legendary King Minos; what they called themselves is unknown. Their script, Linear A, is undeciphered. Mycenaean Greeks took over Knossos about 1450 BCE.

entries.name: Mycenaean Greece
entries.summary: Warrior kingdoms ruled from fortified palaces at Mycenae, Pylos and Tiryns. Their scribes wrote an early form of Greek in the Linear B script, deciphered by Michael Ventris in 1952. The gold mask found at Mycenae was named for Agamemnon, though it is centuries older than the Trojan War of tradition. The palaces were destroyed around 1200 BCE.

entries.name: Classical Greece
entries.summary: Classical Greece was a world of rival city-states, not one empire. Athens developed democracy, drama and philosophy, with Socrates, Plato and Aristotle; Sparta was its great military rival. Together the Greeks fought off Persian invasions at Marathon and Salamis. The age ends with the conquests of Alexander of Macedon, who died in 323 BCE.

entries.name: Alexander’s empire
entries.summary: Alexander III of Macedon, taught by Aristotle, became king at twenty in 336 BCE. In eleven years he conquered the Persian Empire, Egypt and lands to the Indus, founding cities named Alexandria. His army refused to go further at the Beas river in India. He died in Babylon in 323 BCE, and his generals split the empire into kingdoms.

entries.name: Byzantine Empire
entries.summary: The eastern half of the Roman Empire, ruled from Constantinople, which Constantine founded in 330. Its people called themselves Romans. Justinian rewrote the law code and built the Hagia Sophia. For a thousand years it guarded the routes between Europe and Asia and spread Orthodox Christianity to the Slavs, until the Ottomans took Constantinople in 1453.

entries.name: Fall of Constantinople
entries.summary: The Ottoman Sultan Mehmed II besieged Constantinople for about seven weeks and took it on 29 May 1453, after huge cannon battered its ancient land walls. The last emperor, Constantine XI, died in the fighting, ending the Byzantine Empire. The city, later known as Istanbul, became the Ottoman capital, and the Hagia Sophia became a mosque.

entries.name: Carthage
entries.note: The founding date is traditional.
entries.summary: Founded, by tradition in 814 BCE, by Phoenician settlers from Tyre, Carthage grew into a sea power with trading posts across North Africa, Spain, Sardinia and western Sicily. It fought Rome in three Punic Wars; its general Hannibal crossed the Alps with elephants in 218 BCE. Rome destroyed the city in 146 BCE.

entries.name: Roman Republic
entries.summary: After expelling its last king in 509 BCE, Rome was governed by elected magistrates, the consuls, and a Senate. The Republic conquered Italy, defeated Carthage in the Punic Wars and came to rule the Mediterranean. Civil wars in its last century, through Julius Caesar’s dictatorship, ended with Augustus becoming the first emperor in 27 BCE.

entries.name: Roman Empire
entries.note: To the fall of the Western Empire. The Eastern Empire carried on as the Byzantine Empire.
entries.summary: Augustus became the first emperor in 27 BCE. At its height the empire stretched from Britain to Mesopotamia, held together by roads, law, the Latin language and a professional army. Roman merchants traded with India for pepper and cloth. Christianity became its official religion in the 4th century. The western half fell in 476.

entries.name: Viking Age
entries.summary: From the raid on Lindisfarne in 793, Norse seafarers from Scandinavia raided, traded and settled from Russia to Ireland. They founded Dublin, ruled much of England as the Danelaw and gave their name to Normandy. Leif Erikson reached North America about 1000 CE. The age is usually ended in 1066, when Harald Hardrada fell in England.

entries.name: Carolingian Empire
entries.summary: Charlemagne, king of the Franks, was crowned emperor by the Pope in Rome on Christmas Day 800. His empire covered much of western Europe, and his court encouraged learning, with scholars such as Alcuin copying classical texts in a clear new script. His grandsons divided the empire in 843, and it broke apart for good after 888.

entries.name: Holy Roman Empire
entries.summary: Otto I, king of Germany, was crowned emperor in 962, reviving Charlemagne’s title. The empire became a patchwork of hundreds of states in central Europe, under an emperor chosen by leading princes, the electors. The Protestant Reformation began within it, with Martin Luther. After defeats by Napoleon, the last emperor, Francis II, dissolved it in 1806.

entries.name: Napoleonic French Empire
entries.summary: Napoleon Bonaparte, a general who rose in the French Revolution, crowned himself emperor in 1804. His armies won at Austerlitz and redrew the map of Europe, ending the Holy Roman Empire in 1806, and his legal code still shapes laws in many countries. Defeat in Russia in 1812 broke his power; he was finally beaten at Waterloo in 1815.

entries.name: Kievan Rus’
entries.summary: A state of East Slavs and Norse settlers ruled from Kyiv by Rurikid princes. Grand Prince Volodymyr converted to Orthodox Christianity about 988, bringing in Byzantine religion, art and the Cyrillic script. Divided among quarrelling princes, it fell to the Mongols, who sacked Kyiv in 1240. Ukraine, Belarus and Russia all trace their history to it.

entries.name: Muscovy
entries.summary: Moscow rose from a minor town paying tribute to the Mongol Golden Horde. Ivan III threw off Mongol rule in 1480 and called himself sovereign of all Russia; Ivan IV, ‘the Terrible’, was crowned the first tsar in 1547. After the Time of Troubles the Romanov dynasty took the throne in 1613, and Russian rule spread across Siberia.

entries.name: Russian Empire
entries.summary: Peter the Great took the title of emperor in 1721 after defeating Sweden, and built a new capital, St Petersburg. Catherine the Great pushed the empire to the Black Sea, and it stretched from the Baltic to the Pacific, the largest country in the world. Serfdom was abolished in 1861. Revolution in 1917 ended the rule of the Romanovs.

entries.name: Portuguese Empire
entries.summary: Portugal’s empire began with the capture of Ceuta in 1415. Its sailors charted Africa’s coast, and Vasco da Gama reached India in 1498, opening a sea route to Asia. It held Brazil, Goa, Malacca, Macau, Angola and Mozambique, and carried enslaved Africans across the Atlantic on a vast scale. Handing Macau to China in 1999 ended it.

entries.name: Spanish Empire
entries.note: From Columbus to Spain’s withdrawal from Western Sahara in 1976. Estimates of deaths in the Americas vary widely and are disputed.
entries.summary: Columbus’s voyage for Castile in 1492 began an empire that conquered the Aztec and Inca states and ruled from California to Chile, and the Philippines in Asia. Silver from mines such as Potosí paid for its wars in Europe, while epidemics killed a large share of the Americas’ people. Most of Spanish America won independence in the 1810s and 1820s.

entries.name: Columbus reaches the Americas
entries.summary: Sailing west for the Spanish crowns to reach Asia, Christopher Columbus landed in the Bahamas on 12 October 1492, then reached Cuba and Hispaniola. He believed to the end that he had reached Asia. His voyages began lasting contact between Europe and the Americas, with conquest, settlement, the exchange of crops and animals, and deadly epidemics.

entries.name: Vasco da Gama reaches India
entries.summary: Sailing round the Cape of Good Hope, Vasco da Gama reached Calicut on the Malabar coast in May 1498, guided across the Arabian Sea by a pilot taken on at Malindi. The sea route let Portugal trade directly in Asian spices, bypassing Venetian and Arab middlemen, and opened the age of European empires in Asia.

entries.name: French colonial empire
entries.note: Ends with the independence of Vanuatu in 1980; France still governs some overseas territories.
entries.summary: France’s empire began with Jacques Cartier’s voyages to Canada from 1534 and the founding of Quebec in 1608. It lost most of North America and its Indian holdings to Britain by 1763, then built a second empire in Africa and Indochina, second only to Britain’s. Wars in Vietnam and Algeria ended most of it by the early 1960s.

entries.name: British Empire
entries.summary: From colonies in North America and the Caribbean, Britain built the largest empire in history, covering about a quarter of the world’s land by the 1920s. Sea power, trade and companies such as the East India Company drove it, ruling India, much of Africa and Australia. Most colonies won independence after 1945; Hong Kong was handed back in 1997.

entries.name: Dutch colonial empire
entries.summary: The Dutch East India Company (VOC), founded in 1602, was among the world’s first large joint-stock companies. From Batavia (Jakarta) it controlled the spice trade of the East Indies, and the Dutch held Ceylon, the Cape, New Amsterdam (later New York) and Suriname. Indonesia won independence in 1949, after a war, and Suriname in 1975.

entries.name: Qin dynasty
entries.summary: Qin Shi Huang conquered the rival Warring States and in 221 BCE became the first emperor of a united China. He standardised writing, weights, coins and axle widths, and linked earlier walls into a northern defence. He was buried with an army of terracotta warriors. His harsh rule collapsed within a few years of his death.

entries.name: Han dynasty
entries.summary: The Han dynasty gave its name to China’s largest ethnic group. Emperor Wu expanded the empire and made Confucian learning the basis of government service. The envoy Zhang Qian’s journeys west helped open the Silk Road. Paper was invented in this period, and the historian Sima Qian wrote his great history of China.

entries.name: Sui dynasty
entries.summary: The Sui reunited China in 589 after nearly three centuries of division. In under forty years they built the Grand Canal linking the Yangtze and Yellow rivers, rebuilt walls in the north and revived examinations for officials. Costly wars in Korea and heavy demands for labour led to revolt, and the Tang took over in 618.

entries.name: Tang dynasty
entries.summary: Often called a golden age of China. From Chang’an, then one of the largest cities in the world, the Tang ruled far into Central Asia. Wu Zetian ruled as China’s only woman emperor. Li Bai and Du Fu wrote much-loved poetry, and woodblock printing spread. The An Lushan rebellion of 755 left the dynasty weakened.

entries.name: Song dynasty
entries.summary: The Song oversaw a great age of invention and trade: movable-type printing, the magnetic compass at sea, gunpowder weapons and the first paper money issued by a government. Neo-Confucian thinkers such as Zhu Xi shaped learning for centuries. The Jurchen took northern China in 1127, and the Mongols conquered the south in 1279.

entries.name: Yuan dynasty
entries.summary: Kublai Khan, grandson of Genghis Khan, founded the Yuan and ruled China from Dadu, today’s Beijing. The Mongol empire made travel across Asia easier, and Marco Polo described Kublai’s court. Kublai’s invasions of Japan failed. Floods, famine and rebellion ended Mongol rule, and the Ming drove them north in 1368.

entries.name: Ming dynasty
entries.summary: Founded by Zhu Yuanzhang, a former peasant and monk, after driving out the Mongols. The Ming built the Forbidden City in Beijing and most of the Great Wall that stands today. Admiral Zheng He led huge treasure fleets as far as India, Arabia and East Africa, and Ming blue-and-white porcelain was prized across the world.

entries.name: Qing dynasty
entries.summary: The Manchus from the north-east founded the Qing and took Beijing in 1644. Under the Kangxi and Qianlong emperors China reached its largest extent. In the 19th century the Opium Wars with Britain, the Taiping Rebellion and foreign pressure weakened it. The revolution of 1911 ended imperial rule, and the last emperor, Puyi, abdicated in 1912.

entries.name: Mongol Empire
entries.note: Split into khanates after about 1260; 1368 is the fall of the Yuan dynasty in China.
entries.summary: Temüjin was proclaimed Genghis Khan of the united Mongols in 1206. He and his heirs built the largest land empire in history, from Korea to Hungary; their conquests killed very many people, though estimates are disputed. The empire eased trade along the Silk Road. By 1294 it had split into four khanates, and the Yuan in China fell in 1368.

entries.name: Timurid Empire
entries.summary: Timur (Tamerlane), a Turco-Mongol warlord, conquered from Anatolia to Delhi, which he sacked in 1398, at the cost of huge numbers of lives. He filled his capital Samarkand with blue-domed buildings. His descendants, among them the astronomer king Ulugh Beg, made Samarkand and Herat centres of art and science. Babur, a Timurid prince, founded the Mughal Empire.

entries.name: Silla
entries.note: The founding date is traditional.
entries.summary: Silla, by tradition founded in 57 BCE in south-east Korea, was one of the Three Kingdoms with Goguryeo and Baekje. Allied with Tang China, it defeated both rivals by 668 and united most of the peninsula. From its capital Gyeongju it built the Bulguksa temple and the Seokguram grotto. Weakened by revolts, it surrendered to Goryeo in 935.

entries.name: Goryeo
entries.summary: Goryeo, which gives Korea its English name, united the peninsula after Silla. Its potters made celebrated celadon ware, and its monks carved the whole Buddhist canon on more than 80,000 woodblocks, the Tripitaka Koreana. In 1377 a temple printed the Jikji, the oldest surviving book made with movable metal type. Mongol invasions made it a vassal of the Yuan.

entries.name: Joseon
entries.summary: Founded by the general Yi Seong-gye, Joseon ruled Korea for five centuries from Hanyang (Seoul) as a Confucian state. King Sejong the Great introduced the Korean alphabet (hangul) in 1446. Admiral Yi Sun-sin’s armoured ‘turtle ships’ helped repel Japanese invasions in the 1590s. Joseon became the Korean Empire in 1897, which Japan annexed in 1910.

entries.name: Heian Japan
entries.summary: Japan’s emperors moved their capital to Heian-kyō (Kyoto) in 794, while real power passed to the Fujiwara family of regents. Court women wrote in the new kana script: Murasaki Shikibu’s Tale of Genji, often called the world’s first novel, and Sei Shōnagon’s Pillow Book. Wars between the Taira and Minamoto clans ended the age.

entries.name: Kamakura shogunate
entries.summary: After the Minamoto won the Genpei War, Minamoto no Yoritomo set up a military government at Kamakura and in 1192 became shogun, while emperors stayed in Kyoto. Warriors (samurai) became the ruling class, and Zen and Pure Land Buddhism spread. Typhoons, later called kamikaze, ‘divine winds’, helped wreck Mongol invasions in 1274 and 1281.

entries.name: Ashikaga shogunate
entries.summary: Ashikaga Takauji set up a new shogunate in Kyoto’s Muromachi district. Its shoguns built the Golden and Silver Pavilions and encouraged Noh drama, ink painting and the tea ceremony. Their power faded in the Ōnin War from 1467, and Japan broke into rival warlords’ domains. Oda Nobunaga drove out the last Ashikaga shogun in 1573.

entries.name: Tokugawa shogunate
entries.summary: Tokugawa Ieyasu won the Battle of Sekigahara in 1600 and became shogun in 1603, ruling from Edo (Tokyo). For 250 years Japan was at peace and largely closed to foreigners, trading only with the Dutch and Chinese at Nagasaki. Woodblock prints, kabuki and haiku flourished. US warships forced Japan open in 1853; the shogunate fell in 1868.

entries.name: Srivijaya
entries.note: Its beginning and end are uncertain.
entries.summary: From Palembang on Sumatra, Srivijaya controlled the Strait of Malacca and the sea trade between India and China. The Chinese monk Yijing studied there in the 670s and found over a thousand Buddhist monks. A Chola naval raid in 1025 weakened it, and it faded in the 13th century as Javanese and Thai powers rose.

entries.name: Khmer Empire
entries.summary: In 802 Jayavarman II proclaimed himself universal king, founding the Khmer Empire in today’s Cambodia. Its kings built hundreds of temples around Angkor; Suryavarman II’s Angkor Wat is the largest religious monument in the world. Huge reservoirs (barays) watered its rice fields. After a Thai army sacked Angkor in 1431, the capital moved south.

entries.name: Majapahit
entries.summary: Founded on Java in 1293, after a Mongol invasion was driven off, Majapahit became the greatest power of the Indonesian islands. Its chief minister Gajah Mada swore an oath not to rest until the archipelago was united. The court poem Nagarakretagama describes its splendour. It declined as Muslim sultanates such as Demak rose, and fell about 1527.

entries.name: Sumer
entries.note: Dates follow the usual middle chronology and are approximate.
entries.summary: In southern Iraq, between the Tigris and Euphrates, the Sumerians built some of the first cities, such as Uruk and Ur, and one of the first scripts, cuneiform, pressed into clay. They raised temple towers (ziggurats) and told the earliest stories of Gilgamesh. Rival city-states fought for centuries; the fall of Ur about 2004 BCE ended Sumerian rule.

entries.name: Invention of cuneiform
entries.summary: Scribes at Uruk in southern Mesopotamia began pressing signs into clay tablets with reeds, first to keep accounts of grain, animals and workers. The signs became wedge-shaped cuneiform, used for some 3,000 years to write Sumerian, Akkadian, Hittite, Elamite and other languages, from laws and letters to the Epic of Gilgamesh. Egypt’s hieroglyphs appeared at about the same time.

entries.name: Akkadian Empire
entries.summary: Sargon of Akkad united the cities of Mesopotamia about 2334 BCE, in what is often called the first empire. He boasted that ships from Meluhha, probably the Indus region, moored at his capital. His daughter Enheduanna, a high priestess, is the earliest author known by name. The empire collapsed about 2154 BCE, amid drought and invasion.

entries.name: Third Dynasty of Ur
entries.summary: Ur-Nammu reunited Sumer, began the great ziggurat of Ur and gave his name to the oldest surviving law code. His son Shulgi ran the kingdom through governors and armies of scribes, whose tens of thousands of tablets survive. The Elamites sacked Ur about 2004 BCE and carried off its last king, a disaster mourned in the Lament for Ur.

entries.name: Old Babylonian kingdom
entries.summary: Babylon rose under its first dynasty, founded by Amorite kings. Hammurabi, about 1792 to 1750 BCE, conquered most of Mesopotamia and set up a law code, carved on a stone pillar now in the Louvre, with its famous ‘an eye for an eye’. Babylonian scribes advanced mathematics and astronomy. A Hittite raid sacked Babylon in 1595 BCE.

entries.name: Hittite Empire
entries.summary: From their capital Hattusa in central Anatolia, the Hittites ruled one of the great powers of the Bronze Age. They wrote an Indo-European language in cuneiform and were famed for their chariots. After fighting Ramesses II of Egypt at Kadesh, they made one of the earliest known peace treaties, about 1259 BCE. The empire collapsed about 1180 BCE.

entries.name: Kassite Babylonia
entries.summary: The Kassites, probably from the Zagros mountains, ruled Babylonia for about four centuries, longer than any other dynasty there. Their own language is barely known, but they kept Babylon’s gods and scribal schools alive and built a new city, Dur-Kurigalzu. Their kings wrote to Egypt’s pharaohs as equals in the Amarna letters. An Elamite invasion ended their rule.

entries.name: Neo-Assyrian Empire
entries.summary: From cities such as Nineveh and Nimrud, Assyrian kings built the largest empire the world had yet seen, from Egypt to western Iran, with a feared army and mass deportations of conquered peoples. Carved palace reliefs show their wars and hunts. Ashurbanipal gathered a great library of clay tablets. Babylonians and Medes destroyed Nineveh in 612 BCE.

entries.name: Neo-Babylonian Empire
entries.summary: Nabopolassar freed Babylon from Assyria and, with the Medes, destroyed it. His son Nebuchadnezzar II rebuilt Babylon with the blue-glazed Ishtar Gate, took Jerusalem about 587 BCE and carried many of its people into exile. The Hanging Gardens, said to be his, have never been found. Cyrus of Persia took Babylon in 539 BCE.

entries.name: Achaemenid Persia
entries.summary: Cyrus the Great founded the first Persian empire, the largest the world had yet seen, reaching from Egypt and Anatolia to the Indus. Darius I organised it into provinces (satrapies) linked by a royal road, and built Persepolis. The Persians fought the Greeks at Marathon and Salamis. Alexander of Macedon conquered the empire in 330 BCE.

entries.name: Seleucid Empire
entries.summary: Seleucus, one of Alexander’s generals, took the eastern half of his empire, from Syria to Afghanistan. He traded his Indian lands to Chandragupta Maurya for 500 war elephants. Greek cities such as Antioch spread Greek culture across western Asia. Parthians and Romans whittled the empire down until Rome ended it in 63 BCE.

entries.name: Parthian Empire
entries.summary: The Parthians, horsemen from north-east Iran, took Iran and Mesopotamia from the Seleucids and ruled from Ctesiphon. Famous for mounted archers and the ‘Parthian shot’, fired while riding away, they crushed a Roman army at Carrhae in 53 BCE. Their empire sat astride the Silk Road between Rome and China. It fell to the Sasanians in 224 CE.

entries.name: Sasanian Empire
entries.summary: The last Persian empire before Islam, founded by Ardashir I. The Sasanians were Rome’s great rival for four centuries, and Shapur I captured the Roman emperor Valerian. Under Khosrow I learning flourished, and Indian works such as the Panchatantra were translated into Persian. Arab Muslim armies conquered the empire by 651.

entries.name: Rashidun Caliphate
entries.summary: After the Prophet Muhammad’s death in 632, the first four caliphs, Abu Bakr, Umar, Uthman and Ali, led the Muslim community from Medina. Arab armies took Syria, Egypt, Iraq and most of the Sasanian Empire within two decades. Under Uthman the Quran was set down in one standard text. Civil war followed, and Ali was killed in 661.

entries.name: Umayyad Caliphate
entries.summary: Ruling from Damascus, the Umayyads made the caliphate an empire stretching from Spain to the Indus. They built the Dome of the Rock in Jerusalem and made Arabic the language of government. In 711 their armies entered both Spain and Sindh. The Abbasids overthrew them in 750; a survivor founded a new Umayyad state in Spain.

entries.name: Abbasid Caliphate
entries.summary: The Abbasids overthrew the Umayyads and built Baghdad as their capital. Its House of Wisdom translated Greek, Persian and Indian works, and scholars such as al-Khwarizmi spread Indian numerals and algebra. Harun al-Rashid’s court lives on in the Thousand and One Nights. The Mongols sacked Baghdad in 1258, ending the caliphate there.

entries.name: Ottoman Empire
entries.summary: Founded by Osman I in Anatolia, the Ottomans took Constantinople in 1453 and made it their capital. Under Suleiman the Magnificent the empire ruled south-eastern Europe, the Middle East and North Africa, and was famed for its law and for architecture such as the mosques of Sinan. Defeat in the First World War led to its end in 1922.

entries.name: Safavid Empire
entries.summary: Shah Ismail I founded the Safavid dynasty in 1501 and made Shia Islam the faith of Iran, shaping its identity to this day. Shah Abbas I rebuilt Isfahan as his capital, with the great Naqsh-e Jahan square, mosques and bridges, and fought the Ottomans. Afghan invaders took Isfahan in 1722, and the dynasty ended in 1736.

entries.name: Pharaonic Egypt
entries.note: From the first kings of a united Egypt to Alexander’s conquest.
entries.summary: For nearly three thousand years kings (pharaohs) ruled a united Egypt along the Nile. They built the pyramids of Giza and the temples of Karnak, and wrote in hieroglyphs. Famous rulers include Khufu, Hatshepsut, Akhenaten, Tutankhamun and Ramesses II. Persian conquests and finally Alexander of Macedon, in 332 BCE, ended native rule.

entries.name: Great Pyramid of Giza
entries.summary: King Khufu’s tomb at Giza, built of some 2.3 million stone blocks, stood about 146 metres tall and was the tallest building on Earth for about 3,800 years. Logbooks found at Wadi al-Jarf record crews shipping its limestone from the Tura quarries. It is the oldest of the Seven Wonders of the ancient world, and the only one still standing.

entries.name: Battle of Kadesh
entries.summary: Ramesses II of Egypt and Muwatalli II of the Hittites fought near Kadesh, in today’s Syria, in one of the largest chariot battles known. Both sides claimed victory, but Kadesh stayed Hittite. About fifteen years later, Ramesses and Hattusili III agreed one of the earliest known peace treaties, with copies in Egyptian and in Akkadian.

entries.name: Kingdom of Kush
entries.summary: South of Egypt, in today’s Sudan, the kings of Kush ruled from Napata and later Meroë. In the 8th century BCE King Piye conquered Egypt; his family ruled it as the 25th Dynasty. At Meroë they built more pyramids than Egypt, and wrote a Meroitic script that can be sounded out but not understood. Kush declined by about 350 CE.

entries.name: Ptolemaic Egypt
entries.summary: After Alexander’s death his general Ptolemy took Egypt and founded a Greek-speaking dynasty that ruled as pharaohs. Its capital, Alexandria, had the great Library and the Pharos lighthouse, and became the centre of Greek learning. The last of the line, Cleopatra VII, died in 30 BCE, and Egypt became part of the Roman Empire.

entries.name: Kingdom of Aksum
entries.summary: A trading kingdom in today’s Ethiopia and Eritrea, linking the Red Sea with Arabia, India and Rome. Aksum minted its own coins and raised tall carved stone pillars (stelae). King Ezana adopted Christianity in the 4th century, one of the first rulers anywhere to do so. Changing trade routes after the rise of Islam led to its decline.

entries.name: Ghana Empire (Wagadu)
entries.note: Its beginnings are uncertain; Arab writers mention it from the 8th century.
entries.summary: In the Sahel, in today’s Mauritania and Mali, the Soninke kingdom of Wagadu grew rich taxing the gold and salt trade across the Sahara. Arab writers called it Ghana, after its king’s title, and described a capital of two towns, one for the king and one for Muslim merchants. It declined in the 11th and 12th centuries.

entries.name: Great Zimbabwe
entries.summary: Ancestors of the Shona built Great Zimbabwe, a city of massive stone walls laid without mortar. It grew rich on gold and ivory traded to the coast and on to Arabia, India and China. Colonial-era writers wrongly credited it to outsiders; archaeology showed it was African. The country of Zimbabwe takes its name from it.

entries.name: Mali Empire
entries.summary: Sundiata Keita founded Mali, which grew rich on West Africa’s gold and salt trade. Its most famous king, Mansa Musa, made a pilgrimage to Mecca in 1324 with so much gold that he became famous across the Mediterranean world. Timbuktu became a centre of Islamic learning, with the Sankore mosque and many manuscripts.

entries.name: Songhai Empire
entries.summary: Sunni Ali, a warrior king, took Timbuktu in 1468 and built Songhai into the largest empire in West African history, along the Niger river. Askia Muhammad made pilgrimage to Mecca and made Timbuktu and Gao famous centres of trade and Islamic learning. A Moroccan army armed with guns defeated Songhai at Tondibi in 1591.

entries.name: Maya civilisation
entries.note: Millions of Maya people live in the region today and speak Maya languages.
entries.summary: In southern Mexico and Central America the Maya built city-states such as Tikal, Palenque and Copán, with stepped pyramids and ballcourts. They developed the fullest writing system of the ancient Americas, now largely read, an accurate calendar and a sign for zero. Many lowland cities emptied after about 900 CE; the last kingdom fell to Spain in 1697.

entries.name: Olmec
entries.note: Olmec is a modern name, from an Aztec word for the people of the rubber country.
entries.summary: On the Gulf coast of Mexico, the Olmecs built the first great centres of Mesoamerica, at San Lorenzo and La Venta. They carved colossal stone heads up to about three metres tall, probably portraits of rulers. Traditions found across later Mesoamerica, such as the ballgame played with a rubber ball, appear here early. What they called themselves is unknown.

entries.name: Teotihuacan
entries.summary: Teotihuacan, near today’s Mexico City, was among the world’s largest cities around 500 CE, with perhaps 100,000 people; estimates vary. Its Avenue of the Dead runs past the Pyramids of the Sun and Moon; its influence reached Maya cities far to the south. It was burned and largely abandoned by about 550; its own name is unknown.

entries.name: Toltecs (Tula)
entries.note: Dates for Tula’s rise and fall are approximate, and how far Toltec power reached is debated.
entries.summary: From Tula, in today’s Hidalgo, the Toltecs were a leading power of central Mexico between about 900 and 1150. Their capital, Tollan, is known for its stone columns carved as warriors and its colonnaded halls. The later Aztecs remembered them as the inventors of every art and claimed their blood; stories of a priest-king, Quetzalcoatl, are set at Tula.

entries.name: Aztec Empire
entries.summary: The Mexica founded Tenochtitlan on an island in Lake Texcoco, by their own account in 1325. In 1428 they formed the Triple Alliance with Texcoco and Tlacopan, which came to rule much of central Mexico through tribute. Tenochtitlan, with its causeways, floating gardens (chinampas) and Templo Mayor, astonished the Spanish. Hernán Cortés and his Indigenous allies took it in 1521.

entries.name: Fall of Tenochtitlan
entries.summary: After a siege of nearly three months, Hernán Cortés’s Spanish troops and tens of thousands of Indigenous allies, above all from Tlaxcala, took Tenochtitlan on 13 August 1521. Smallpox, brought by the Spanish, had already killed many of its people, including the emperor Cuitláhuac. The last emperor, Cuauhtémoc, was captured. Mexico City was built on its ruins.

entries.name: Fall of Nojpetén
entries.summary: On 13 March 1697 a Spanish force under Martín de Ursúa crossed Lake Petén Itzá in a galley and took Nojpetén, the island capital of the Itza, the last independent Maya kingdom. The Itza king, Kan Ek’, was captured. Nojpetén is now the town of Flores, Guatemala; Maya resistance in the forests went on for years.

entries.name: The Popol Vuh
entries.summary: The Popol Vuh, the council book of the K’iche’ Maya, was written down in the 1550s in K’iche’ in Latin letters. It tells how the gods, after failing with mud and wood, made people from maize, and how the Hero Twins, Hunahpu and Xbalanque, beat the lords of the underworld (Xibalba) at the ballgame.

entries.name: The eagle on the cactus
entries.summary: Mexica tradition tells how their god Huitzilopochtli led them for generations from Aztlan and promised a sign where they should settle: an eagle on a prickly pear cactus growing from a rock. They saw it on a marshy island in Lake Texcoco and founded Tenochtitlan there, by tradition in 1325. The eagle, cactus and snake are on Mexico’s flag.

entries.name: Chavín
entries.summary: Chavín de Huántar, a temple centre high in the Peruvian Andes, drew pilgrims from far away. Its stone galleries hold the Lanzón, a carved fanged idol, and its art of jaguars, eagles and serpents spread across much of Peru. It may have housed an oracle; how it was governed is unknown. Its influence faded by about 200 BCE.

entries.name: Moche
entries.summary: On Peru’s dry north coast, the Moche irrigated desert valleys and built huge adobe pyramids, the Huacas of the Sun and Moon. Their potters made lifelike portrait vessels and scenes of daily life and ritual. The tomb of the Lord of Sipán, found unlooted in 1987, revealed their gold and turquoise work. Floods and drought may have hastened their end.

entries.name: Tiwanaku
entries.summary: Near Lake Titicaca, at about 3,850 metres, the city of Tiwanaku was the centre of a power that reached into today’s Peru, Chile and Bolivia. Its builders cut and fitted huge stones, as in the Gateway of the Sun, and farmed on raised fields that resisted frost. A long drought around 1000 CE probably helped bring its decline.

entries.name: Inca Empire (Tawantinsuyu)
entries.note: 1438 is the traditional start of Pachacuti’s reign; the last Inca stronghold fell in 1572.
entries.summary: From Cusco, Pachacuti and his heirs built the largest empire of the Americas, Tawantinsuyu, stretching some 4,000 kilometres along the Andes. Roads tens of thousands of kilometres long, rope bridges and relay runners held it together, and records were kept on knotted cords (khipu). They built Machu Picchu. Civil war and smallpox had weakened it before Pizarro arrived.

entries.name: Pizarro captures Atahualpa
entries.summary: On 16 November 1532 Francisco Pizarro, with fewer than 200 Spanish soldiers, ambushed the Inca emperor Atahualpa and his largely unarmed retinue in the square of Cajamarca; accounts say thousands were killed. Atahualpa paid a room full of gold and silver as ransom but was executed in 1533. The last Inca stronghold, Vilcabamba, fell in 1572.

entries.name: Mississippian culture
entries.summary: Across the Mississippi valley and the south-east of North America, farming peoples grew maize and built towns around great earthen mounds. The largest, Cahokia, near today’s St Louis, may have held 10,000 to 20,000 people around 1100 CE, though estimates vary; its Monks Mound is the biggest earthwork of the ancient Americas. Many towns had emptied before Europeans arrived.

entries.name: The Silk Road
entries.summary: Not one road but a web of land and sea routes linking China, Central Asia, India, Persia and the Mediterranean. Silk, spices, horses, paper and glass travelled along them, and so did Buddhism, Islam, ideas and disease. Han China’s envoys helped open the overland routes in the 2nd century BCE.
